trigger.stated_reason: Farage announced he would vacate the seat and re-contest it himself, saying he wanted Clacton voters rather than the press or parliamentary authorities to decide whether he continues as their MP. The announcement came amid a Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards investigation into his financial interests, including a reported 5 million pound payment from Christopher Harborne (also flagged to the National Crime Agency under the Suspicious Activity Report scheme), alleged cryptocurrency lobbying of the Bank of England, and property declarations.

contest.precedent_note: Resign-and-recontest has form in Clacton itself: Douglas Carswell resigned and re-won the seat for UKIP at the 2014 Clacton by-election. Mark Reckless (Rochester and Strood 2014) and Zac Goldsmith (Richmond Park 2016) are the other modern precedents. A win does not end the standards investigation: suspension, recall and a further by-election all remain possible afterwards.

boycott.note: All five parties confirmed within days of the writ that they will not contest the by-election, framing it as unnecessary and self-inflicted. Kemi Badenoch called it 'Farage's fake by-election'. Restore Britain, the party most directly competing for Reform's vote, also declined to stand.

field.record_note: A record 34 candidates were nominated, the most for any UK by-election, beating the 26 who stood at Haltemprice and Howden in 2008. The size of the field is a direct product of the major-party boycott: with no mainstream opponent on the ballot, minor parties, independents and novelty candidates filled the vacuum.

candidates.note: Party leader; MP for Clacton July 2024 to July 2026. Won the seat at GE2024 with 46.2%. The overwhelming favourite.

The de-facto main challenger given the boycott. Raised over 15,000 pounds within a day; green-energy industrialist Dale Vince offered to fund the campaign. An Ipsos 'who do you want to win' poll put Binface on 33% to Farage's 21%, a novelty-driven question rather than a turnout-modelled vote-intention figure.

forecast.headline: No vote-share forecast. With Labour, the Conservatives, the Liberal Democrats, the Greens and Restore Britain all standing aside, no mainstream opponent is on the ballot. Farage is the overwhelming favourite: psephologist John Curtice expects him to win comfortably in a seat that voted roughly 75% Leave in 2016. The only genuinely open question is turnout, in mid-August with the result a foregone conclusion.
open_questions: Turnout: an August by-election with no mainstream contest is likely to be low; the 2014 Carswell by-election (also a Clacton resign-and-recontest) drew 51.0%.

The runner-up: with the field a record 34 candidates and no major party standing, second place is a real contest between Count Binface, minor-party and independent candidates. An Ipsos 'who do you want to win' question put Binface ahead of Farage, but that is a novelty measure, not a turnout-weighted vote-intention.
Farage's margin and share versus his 46.2% at GE2024: a lower share against a fractured field would still be a comfortable win but a weaker mandate.
forecast.no_forecast_rationale: Every quantitative method we benchmark (GE swing model, poll of polls, local signal) assumes the major parties contest the seat. A five-party boycott breaks that assumption: national vote-intention shares cannot be mapped onto a ballot missing parties that hold roughly two-thirds of the national vote between them. Publishing invented shares would repeat the Makerfield mistake in a different costume. We will grade the outcome (winner, margin, turnout) against the qualitative call above.
